notes:
# Research notes on Lamentations 5 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**How these notes were gathered:** The main sources were Barnes (biblehub), Ellicott (studylight), David Guzik (enduringword), and the multi-commentary pages on biblehub and studylight (Gill, Keil & Delitzsch, Pulpit, JFB, Poole, Calvin, Matthew Henry, Clarke). I also used the NET Bible notes, a Ligonier devotional and Haydock's Catholic commentary. I didn't get to preceptaustin, and I found nothing from Lutheran, Pentecostal-denominational or Orthodox sites, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are left out.

---

## The chapter as a whole

- **A prayer.** Ellicott says this chapter is more of a prayer than any other in the book, and it opens by listing Judah's sufferings as a reason for God to have pity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- **Why it isn't an acrostic.** It has 22 verses, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, but the verses don't follow alphabetical order (Barnes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
  - Ellicott thinks the poem was meant to become an acrostic and was left half-finished. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
  - Guzik quotes Adam Clarke's suggestion that such a technical form seemed out of place in a time of agony. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/
- **Its title in old versions.** Gill notes that the Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic versions call it "the prayer of Jeremiah." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-1.htm
- **Outline (Ellicott):** first a plea to God, then the misery in the land, the hardships and indignities people suffer, a general despair, and finally an appeal grounded in God's lasting power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-1.htm

---

## Verse by verse

**v. 1 ("Remember")**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the second line ("look and see our disgrace") explains the first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-1.htm
- Guzik: Jeremiah knew God was aware of their suffering, but he understandably *felt* forgotten. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/
- The Expositor's Bible notes the stress falls on humiliation rather than pain, because God's own honour is bound up with his people's ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/5.htm
- Calvin: God is pleased to help the miserable when their troubles are laid out before him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/5-1.html
- Biblehub's study notes: "remember" doesn't imply God forgets. It is a plea for him to act. https://biblehub.com/lamentations/5-1.htm

**v. 2 (land and houses)**
- Barnes: the "inheritance" is the land of Canaan, now passed to the Chaldeans (Babylonians). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott: the Babylonians had burned Jerusalem's houses, so these are probably the homes of farmers and country people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html

**v. 3 (orphans and widows)**
- Barnes: the word "as" shows the verse is a picture. Their desolation is like that of orphans and widows. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott: the husbands were alive but in exile, so the wives were as destitute as widows. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- Guzik quotes Ellison: most of those left in Judah were the very poor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/

**v. 4 (buying water and wood)**
- The sting is in the word "our." They now have to buy what was always theirs (Barnes; Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: water and wood are the basic needs of life, and the enemy now holds the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-4.htm
- **Where was this?** Commentators disagree.
  - JFB, Poole and Gill lean toward life in exile in Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-4.htm
  - Ellicott thinks it fits those left behind in Judah better. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html

**v. 5 (pursued, no rest)**
- Barnes: the enemy seemed to be leaning over their necks, chasing them without a break. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Calvin: having enemies ride on your neck is the worst degradation. He calls it a fitting result for a "stiff-necked" people who refused God's yoke. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-5.html

**v. 6 (Egypt and Assyria)**
- Barnes: "giving the hand" means surrendering. Patriotism was crushed, and people would submit to anyone just to survive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott: "Assyria" stands for Babylon here, and "Egypt" refers to refugees who fled there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- Guzik quotes Wright: Assyria was no longer an empire, so this may look back to the old alliances the prophets had condemned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/

**v. 7 (the fathers' sins)** *(see the debate section below)*
- Barnes: the generation that began the nation's turning from God died before the punishment came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- The NET notes say "punishment for sin" is the best sense of the word here. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Lam+5%3A1-22

**v. 8 (slaves rule)**
- Barnes: being ruled by slaves was a terrible humiliation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott: Babylon may have sent low-ranking court servants to govern them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- The NET notes suggest the phrase may be an idiom for "tyrants rule over us." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Lam+5%3A1-22

**v. 9 (bread and the sword)**
- Barnes and Pulpit: people gathering the leftover harvest were attacked by desert raiders ("Bedouin"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-9.htm
- Gill and Poole place it during the siege instead, with the Babylonian army camped on the plain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-9.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: this fulfils the covenant warnings of Deuteronomy 28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-9.htm

**v. 10 (fever from hunger)**
- Barnes and Ellicott prefer "fiery red" with the fever of famine over the KJV's "black," since the picture is hot fever rather than pale exhaustion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- Guzik quotes Ellison: "scorched" skin shows general starvation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/

**v. 11 (women ravished)**
- The Expositor's Bible: from here the poem moves through each group in society in turn, and neither motherhood nor innocence gave women any protection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/5.htm
- Guzik cites Clarke: Moses and Jeremiah had foretold this (Deuteronomy 28:30, 32; Jeremiah 6:12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/

**v. 12 (princes hung up)**
- Barnes: dead princes' bodies were hung up to shame them publicly, and old age protected no one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott compares the treatment of Saul's body (1 Samuel 31). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- The Expositor's Bible suggests the bodies may have been impaled, as was the Babylonian custom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/5.htm
- Clarke (in Guzik) thinks it was a torture: being hung by the hands until death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/

**v. 13 (millstones and wood)**
- Grinding grain was slaves' or women's work. Ellicott thinks the young men may have had to carry the mills on the march to Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- Ellison (in Guzik): in better days these men would have been soldiers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/
- The NET notes say the Hebrew is difficult. They mention that the Vulgate reads it as a sexual-abuse image, which the notes reject. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Lam+5%3A1-22

**vv. 14–15 (gate, music, dancing)**
- The city gate was where elders met to give counsel and judgment and to talk. The music and dancing were the young people's joys, now cut off (Ellicott; Barnes). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html

**v. 16 (the crown has fallen)**
- Barnes: the "crown" is the nation's independence and honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott: this personal confession contrasts with the half-complaining tone of v. 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- The Expositor's Bible: the poet moves from shame to sin, because humiliation breaks down the pride that blocks conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/5.htm

**vv. 17–18 (faint hearts, jackals on Zion)**
- Ellicott: "this" points to the lost honour of v. 16, and "these things" to the horrors of vv. 8–15. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html
- Calvin: sorrow is joined to admitting sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/lamentations-5.html
- Barnes: the "foxes" are better called jackals, animals that live in ruins and avoid people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm

**v. 19 (God reigns forever)**
- Barnes: the earthly sanctuary is in ruins, but God's heavenly throne remains. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/lamentations/5.htm
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is literally "you sit," that is, enthroned. The mourner takes comfort that God's loving purpose doesn't change. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html

**v. 20 ("Why have you forgotten us?")**
- Guzik: the truth of God's unchanging nature had not yet been *felt* in their situation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/
- The NET notes: "forget" is a figure of speech. God's judgment was so long and intense that it seemed he had forgotten Jerusalem existed. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Lam+5%3A1-22

**v. 21 ("Restore us… so we may return")** *(see the debate section below)*
- The NET notes: the Hebrew repeats the verb *shuv* ("turn/return"), which pictures a two-way relationship between God's willingness and the nation's repentance. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Lam+5%3A1-22

**v. 22 ("unless…")** *(see the debate section below)*
- In synagogue reading, v. 21 is repeated after v. 22 so the book doesn't end on such a dark word (Barnes; Ellicott; Keil & Delitzsch). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-22.htm

---

## Where interpreters really differ

**v. 7: are they blaming their fathers?**
- **Complaint view.** Guzik reads it as the popular "sour grapes" saying, which charged God with unfairness. He says Ezekiel 18 answers it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/
- **Not an excuse.** Poole says it shouldn't be read in the same sense as Ezekiel 18:2. The godly speakers aren't excusing themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-7.htm
- **Children who continue the sin.** Keil & Delitzsch: God punishes children who carry on their fathers' sins, not innocent children. The point is to move God to pity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-7.htm
- **A middle view.** Ellicott says the complaint is about a double penalty, and it is balanced by the confession in v. 16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-5.html

**v. 21: a prayer for repentance, or for God's favour?** This is mostly a split *within* the Reformed tradition rather than between denominations.
- **Repentance must come from God.**
  - The Geneva Bible notes: it is not in our power to turn to God. God works in us first. https://www.studylight.org/bible/tgl/ceb/lamentations/5-21.html
  - Matthew Henry: the prayer admits we can't turn ourselves, and God's grace is both necessary and effective. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/lamentations/5.htm
  - Guzik takes the same line, calling it a prayer for the gift of repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/
- **God's favour.** Calvin himself says the verse is *not* about repentance. It is about God turning to receive them back into his favour. JFB repeats Calvin's view but adds that sinners may still use the prayer for their own conversion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-21.htm
- **Wesleyan.** The only line I found from Wesley's *Explanatory Notes* is brief: "Renew" means restore us to our former state. https://www.studylight.org/bible/tgl/ceb/lamentations/5-21.html

**v. 22: how to read "unless"**
- **Stated only to be denied.** Calvin argues from the impossible: God cannot finally reject his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/5-22.html
  - Barnes and Ellicott agree, and so do the Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-22.htm
  - A Ligonier devotional follows Calvin: the "unless" points to God's steadfast covenant love. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/final-plea-restoration
- **Other ways to read it.** Calvin's own translator (in a footnote) and Blayney read the word as "because": God *has* rejected them, which is why they pray. Pareau and Gill read it as a question ("Will you utterly reject us?"). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/5-22.html
- **An open ending.** Guzik says the book ends on an unresolved fear, though history shows God didn't reject Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-5/

---

## Other views

**Modern scholarship (NET notes)**
- On v. 22, the notes treat rejection as a real possibility Jeremiah faces: restoration would be impossible if God had decided to reject the nation for good. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Lam+5%3A1-22

**Catholic**
- The Douay-Rheims translates v. 21 as "Convert us, O Lord, to thee, and we shall be converted." https://biblehub.com/catholic/lamentations/5-21.htm
- Haydock (on the book as a whole, not v. 21 specifically) says the Church reads Lamentations on the anniversary of Christ's passion, calling sinners to repent. He adds that many passages apply to a soul that has fallen into sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/lamentations.html

**An older Christian reading**
- Gill reports that Cocceius applied the whole chapter to the Church's sufferings, though Gill prefers to read it of the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/5-1.htm
